passage.title: How Stories Survive
paras: Every family has stories: how a grandparent crossed a sea, how a street got its name, how a recipe came to be. Most of them are never written down. They live in memory, passed from one voice to the next, and they last only as long as someone keeps telling them.

Long before printing, whole communities kept their knowledge in memory. Muslims preserved the Qur'an both by heart and in writing: many companions memorised it, and it was gathered into a single written copy, then copied and sent to the great cities. Today archives record the voices of elderly people before their memories are lost. The lesson is the same in every age: a story survives only if someone decides it is worth carrying.

Writing is not enough on its own. Books burn, files are lost and languages fade. Memory is not enough either; people forget, and people die. The stories that last are the ones that have both: a record and a community that cares.
So ask the oldest person you know about their childhood. Write it down. Record it if they agree. You may be the person who decides that their story is worth carrying.

questions.q: Extend: explain why oral testimony is valuable to historians
